q: 155. The length of a ranging rod should be
explain: A standard ranging rod is generally made 2 to 3 m long, painted in alternate red and white (or black) bands of 20 cm each for visibility.

q: 156. The principle of optics used in the construction of an optical square is
explain: An optical square works on the principle of double reflection, using two mirrors inclined at 45 deg to each other to deviate a ray of light through exactly 90 deg.

q: 157. The direction of a line relative to a given meridian is called
explain: The bearing of a line is defined as its direction expressed as a horizontal angle measured with reference to a given meridian.

q: 158. A horizontal angle which a line makes with the true meridian through one of the extremities of the line, is called
explain: When the reference meridian used is the true (geographic) meridian, the resulting horizontal angle is specifically called the true bearing of the line.

q: 159. Which of the following instruments can be used for the direct measurement of directions?
explain: Both the surveyor's compass and the prismatic compass are magnetic instruments capable of directly measuring the bearing/direction of a line in the field.

q: 160. Traversing is generally done by
explain: A traverse survey can be carried out using a chain (chain traversing), a compass, a theodolite, or a plane table, depending on the accuracy required, so all methods are applicable.

q: 161. The box of prismatic compass is made of
explain: The box of a prismatic compass is made of non-magnetic brass so that it does not interfere with or attract the freely suspended magnetic needle.

q: 162. If 'n' is the number of sides, then the total sum of interior angles of a closed traverse should be
explain: The sum of interior angles of a closed polygon of n sides is given by the standard geometric formula (2n - 4) x 90 degrees.

q: 163. If 'n' is the number of sides, then the total sum of exterior angles of a closed traverse should be
explain: Since interior and exterior angles at each vertex are supplementary and their total for all n vertices is 4 right angles more than the interior sum, the sum of exterior angles works out to (2n + 4) x 90 degrees.

q: 164. If the end stations of a line are free from local attraction, then the difference in between fore and back bearing of that line should be
explain: In the absence of local attraction at either end station, the fore bearing and back bearing of a line always differ by exactly 180 degrees.

q: 165. The imaginary line joining the points if zero declination on the surface of the earth is called as
explain: The agonic line is the specific isogonic line that joins points having zero magnetic declination, i.e., where magnetic north coincides with true north.

q: 166. The variation in magnetic declination may be
explain: Magnetic declination is known to vary due to diurnal (daily), annual, and secular (long-term, over years) causes, so all types of variation apply.

q: 167. If the fore bearing of a line is observed to be 12 deg 24', the back bearing of line AB should be
explain: Back bearing = Fore bearing + 180 deg (since FB < 180 deg) = 12 deg 24' + 180 deg = 192 deg 24'.

q: 168. The lines of force of earth's magnetic field are parallel to the earth's surface
options: at right angles to the poles
at 45 deg to the line joining poles
explain: Near the equator, the earth's magnetic field lines run roughly horizontal (parallel to the surface), which is why the dip of the needle is close to zero there; near the poles the field lines are nearly vertical.

q: 169. At magnetic poles, the dip of magnetic needle is
explain: At the magnetic poles, a freely suspended needle aligns itself vertically with the earth's field, giving a dip of 90 degrees.

q: 170. The least count of prismatic compass is
explain: A standard prismatic compass is generally graduated to allow readings to a least count of about 15 minutes of arc.

q: 171. The total number of zeroes graduated on a surveyor's compass is
explain: A surveyor's compass, graduated in the quadrantal bearing system, has two zero marks (at the North and South ends), unlike the prismatic compass which has only a single zero (North) on its whole-circle graduated ring.

q: 172. At the equator, the amount of dip is
explain: At the magnetic equator, the earth's magnetic field lines run horizontal, so a freely suspended needle shows zero dip.

q: 173. The graduated ring of a prismatic compass is graduated in
options: any of the system mentioned above
explain: The prismatic compass has its graduated ring marked continuously from 0 deg to 360 deg, i.e., in the whole circle bearing system.

q: 174. The first temporary adjustment of a prismatic compass is centering, levelling, for all
explain: The very first temporary adjustment carried out for a prismatic compass at each station is centering it exactly over the survey station.

q: 175. Which of the following may not cause local attraction on a magnetic needle?
options: loop of a wire carrying electrical current
explain: Wooden pegs, being non-magnetic and non-conducting, do not cause any local attraction on a compass needle, unlike current-carrying wires or steel objects.

q: 176. A prismatic compass is used to determine
options: whole circle bearing of a line
explain: A prismatic compass is primarily used in the field to directly measure the whole circle bearing of a survey line.

q: 177. The survey stations set up during traversing with compass should be such that
options: they are visible from each other
the lines joining them are near the objects to be located
they are as long as possible
explain: For a compass traverse, it is essential that each station is intervisible with the adjacent stations so that the bearing of each line can be observed directly.

q: 178. The process of putting the plane table into some fixed position so that a line representing certain direction of the plane is parallel to the direction in the field is known as
explain: Orientation is the process of aligning the plane table so that lines drawn on the sheet are parallel to the corresponding lines/directions on the ground.

q: 179. Which one of the following is known as instrumental error in plane table surveying?
explain: Non-horizontality of the plane table board is an instrumental (equipment set-up) error, as distinct from personal errors like defective sighting, orientation, or centering.

q: 180. Accurate centering of a plane table is done by
explain: A plumbing fork (with a plumb bob) is the instrument used to accurately centre the plane table exactly over the ground station point.

q: 181. The working edge of an alidade, is known as
explain: The straight ruling edge of an alidade against which sighting/drawing lines are drawn is specifically called the fiducial edge.

q: 182. In the method of plane table survey the object to be plotted is sighted from two plane table stations. This method is called as
explain: Sighting the same object from two different, known plane table stations and plotting its position at the intersection of the two resulting rays is the method of intersection.

q: 183. Finding the location of the station occupied by the table, on the sheet by means of sighting to three well defined points whose locations have been previously plotted on the sheet, is known as
explain: This specific technique of locating the occupied plane table station using three known, already-plotted points is called the three-point problem.

q: 184. Reading of the metric levelling staff can be taken accurately up to
explain: A metric levelling staff, graduated to 5 mm divisions, can be read accurately to about 0.01 m (10 mm) by estimation between graduations, or precisely to the smallest graduation.

q: 185. The combined correction due to refraction and earth's curvature is
explain: Since the curvature correction (negative, i.e., subtracted from the reading, or rather makes the object appear lower requiring a positive elevation correction) and refraction correction (positive, opposite in sign, smaller in magnitude) partly offset each other, but the net combined effect is applied as a subtractive correction to the staff reading.

q: 186. The errors in levelling due to earths' curvature are
explain: The error introduced by the earth's curvature, if uncorrected, always makes the staff reading appear too great (object appears lower than actual), which is treated as a positive error in the observed reading.

q: 187. When it is not possible to set up the level, midway between the two points, then the difference in elevation between them is measured by
explain: Reciprocal levelling is specifically used when it is impossible to set the instrument midway between two points (e.g., across a river or ravine), allowing errors of curvature, refraction and collimation to be eliminated by observing from both ends.

q: 188. The combined correction for refraction and earth's curvature (in levelling observations) is
explain: The standard formula for combined correction for curvature and refraction (distance d in km) is 0.06735*d2 metres, obtained after applying the standard refraction coefficient to the pure curvature correction of 0.0785*d2.

q: 189. If the back sight and fore sight distance are kept equal during levelling observations, then the effect of both refraction and earth's curvature will be
explain: When back sight and fore sight distances are kept equal, the equal and opposite curvature/refraction errors in both readings cancel out exactly, giving a net effect of zero on the computed difference in level.

q: 190. Personal error in levelling occur due to
explain: Personal errors in levelling arise from the observer's own mistakes, which include careless levelling of the instrument, failing to centre the bubble, and not holding the staff vertical -- so all the listed causes apply.

q: 191. Levelling across a river is done by
explain: Reciprocal levelling is the standard method used to determine the difference in elevation across an obstacle like a river, where the instrument cannot be set up midway.

q: 192. The contours merge or cross one another on the map in case of
explain: Contours merge (coincide) at a vertical cliff surface, and actually cross one another only in the special case of overhanging ground/caves, so all these listed conditions represent exceptions to the normal rule.

q: 193. Contours are used to determine
options: indivisibility of points on a contour map
area of the drainage basin and capacity of the reservoir
explain: Contour maps are versatile tools used to determine intervisibility of points, drainage basin areas and reservoir capacities, and earthwork quantities, so all listed uses apply.

q: 194. Closed contours with higher value inside represents a
explain: When the innermost closed contour has the highest elevation value, it represents a hill (elevated feature).

q: 195. Error in sighting and reading is termed as
explain: Errors arising from the limitations of the observer's own senses in sighting and reading (e.g., estimation errors) are classified as personal errors.

q: 196. According to Bowditch Rule, the correction to latitude (or departure) of any side is equal to
options: Length of the side / Perimeter of traverse
Perimeter of traverse / Length of the side
Total error in latitude / Perimeter of traverse
Total error in latitude x Length of that side / Perimeter of traverse
explain: Bowditch's rule states that the correction to the latitude (or departure) of a side is proportional to the length of that side: Correction = Total error in latitude x (Length of that side / Perimeter of traverse).

q: 197. Which of the following methods of theodolite traversing is suitable for locating the details which are far away from transit stations?
options: by measuring angle to the point from at least three stations
by measuring angles to the point from at least two stations
by measuring angel at one station and distance from other
by measuring distance from two points on traverse line
explain: Distant details, which cannot be directly chained, are located by the method of intersection, measuring angles to the point from at least two known theodolite stations.

q: 198. The spiral angle of a transition curve will be given by the equation
explain: The spiral (deflection) angle of a transition curve at any point is given by the formula phi = L2/(2*R*Ls) which, at the end of a full transition curve of length L, reduces to the standard form L2/2R (for the total spiral length).

q: 199. The curvature of the earth is taken into consideration if the limit of survey is
explain: As with Q1, surveys covering more than about 260 km2 must take the earth's curvature into account and are treated as geodetic surveys.

q: 200. In chain surveying, perpendiculars to the chain line, are set out by
explain: As in Q77, right angles in chain surveying are set out using an optical square (or cross-staff), simple field instruments suited to the linear-only nature of chain survey work.

q: 201. In order to determine the natural features such as valleys, rivers, lakes etc., the surveying preferred is
explain: Topographical surveying is specifically aimed at depicting natural features of the terrain, such as valleys, rivers, and lakes.

q: 202. The surveying used to determine additional details such as boundaries of fields, is called
explain: Cadastral surveying is used to determine and record property/field boundaries and related administrative details.

q: 203. The fundamental principle of surveying is to work from the
explain: As established earlier, the fundamental principle of surveying is to proceed from the whole (a broad framework) down to the part (detailed measurements).

q: 204. The working from whole to the part is done in surveying in order to ensure that
options: survey work is completed more quickly
errors and mistakes of one portion do not affect the remaining portion
explain: Working from whole to part localizes errors, so that any small error made in one part of the survey does not propagate and magnify across the rest of the survey area.

q: 205. When 1 cm on a map represents 10m on the ground, the representative fraction of the scale in
explain: 1 cm represents 10 m = 1000 cm, so the representative fraction is 1/1000.

q: 206. The method of measuring distance by pacing is chiefly used in
explain: Pacing, being a rough and quick method of distance measurement, is chiefly used during preliminary reconnaissance surveys where high accuracy is not required.

q: 207. Direct ranging is possible only when the end stations are
options: located at highest points in the sea
explain: Direct ranging (fixing intermediate points on a line by eye alone) is possible only when the two end stations of the line are mutually intervisible.

q: 208. The error in measured length due to incorrect holding of chain is
explain: Incorrect holding of the chain (not exactly along the line) sometimes lengthens and sometimes shortens the measured length randomly, so it is classified as a compensating (accidental) error.

q: 209. When the length of chain used in measuring distance is longer than the standard length, the error in measured distance will be
explain: If the actual chain is longer than the standard length, fewer chain lengths are needed to cover the true distance, so the recorded (measured) distance comes out less than the true distance, i.e., a negative error.

q: 210. An angle measured clockwise from the proceeding survey line to the following survey line is called
explain: A deflection angle is measured from the prolongation of the preceding line to the following line, and when the direction is clockwise, it is a right deflection angle.

q: 211. In precision theodolite traverse for roads and railways, the angular error of closure should not exceed
explain: For a precision theodolite traverse suitable for roads and railways, the permissible angular error of closure is 1 minute multiplied by the square root of the number of stations (N).

q: 212. The length of a traverse line (L) may be obtained by
options: L = Latitude x secant of reduced bearing
L = Departure x cosecant of reduced bearing
explain: The length of a traverse line can be computed from its latitude and departure using any of several equivalent trigonometric relations, hence any one of the above methods gives the correct length.

q: 213. A staff reading taken on a point whose elevation is to be determined as on a change point is called
explain: A foresight is the last staff reading taken from a given instrument position, typically on a change point whose elevation is being determined before shifting the instrument.

q: 214. Rise and fall method is used in
explain: The rise and fall method of reducing levels is applicable in differential levelling and provides an inherent arithmetic check, and is thus used generally in both differential and check levelling.

q: 215. The method of levelling in which the heights of mountains are found by observing the temperature at which water boils is known as
explain: Hypsometry is the method of determining elevation by observing the boiling point of water, which varies with atmospheric pressure (and hence altitude).

q: 216. The method of surveying used for determining the relative height of points on the surface of the earth is called
explain: Differential levelling is the method specifically used to determine the relative heights (difference in elevation) of points on the earth's surface.

q: 217. A surface which is normal to the direction of gravity at all points, as indicated by a plumb line, is known as
explain: By definition, a level surface is one that is perpendicular to the direction of gravity (the plumb line) at every point on it.

q: 218. An arbitrary surface with reference to which the elevation of points is measured and compared, is called
explain: A datum surface is any arbitrarily chosen level surface used as the reference from which all elevations in a survey are measured.

q: 219. A line normal to the plumb line at all points is known as
explain: A level line, being everywhere perpendicular to the plumb line (direction of gravity), is a curved line following the level surface of the earth.

q: 220. The vertical distance above or below the datum is called
explain: The vertical distance of a point above or below the chosen datum is termed either its 'reduced level' or its 'elevation' -- the two terms are used interchangeably.

q: 221. A fixed point of reference of known elevation is called
explain: A bench mark is, by definition, a fixed point of reference whose elevation is already known and used to start/check levelling operations.

q: 222. An imaginary line tangential to the longitudinal curve of the bubble tube at its middle point is called
explain: The axis of the level tube (bubble tube axis) is the imaginary line tangential to the curved internal surface of the tube at its centre point.

q: 223. A staff reading taken on a bench mark or a point of known elevation is called
explain: A back sight is, by definition, the first staff reading taken from a level setup on a point of already-known elevation, such as a bench mark.

q: 224. The most accurate measurement of the length of a long survey lines is made by using?
explain: Electronic Distance Measuring (EDM) equipment provides the highest accuracy for measuring the length of long survey lines, superior to steel bands, invar tapes, or tacheometry.

q: 225. To find the true difference of level between two points, the level should be kept
options: at either of the two points
exactly midway between the two points
at any point on the line joining the two points
explain: To eliminate the effects of curvature, refraction, and collimation error most effectively, the level should ideally be set up exactly midway between the two points being observed.

q: 226. The height of instrument is equal to
options: reduced level of bench mark + back sight
reduced level of bench mark + fore sight
reduced level of bench mark + intermediate sight
explain: The height of the instrument (H.I.) is calculated by adding the back sight reading to the reduced level of the point on which the back sight was taken (typically a bench mark).

q: 227. A method of differential levelling is used in order to find the difference in elevation between two points when
options: the difference in elevation between them is too great
explain: Differential levelling using a series of intermediate instrument setups is used whenever the two points are too far apart, have obstacles between them, or have too great a difference in elevation to be observed in a single setup -- so all these conditions apply.

q: 228. The collimation method for obtaining the reduced levels of points does not provide a check on
explain: In the collimation (height of instrument) method, intermediate sight reduced levels are computed directly from the H.I. without any independent arithmetic check, unlike fore sights and back sights.

q: 229. The rise and fall method for obtaining the reduced levels of points provides a check on
explain: The rise and fall method computes the rise/fall between every pair of consecutive readings, so it provides a complete arithmetic check on all readings -- back sights, intermediate sights, and fore sights.

q: 230. Reciprocal leveling eliminates
explain: Reciprocal levelling, as noted earlier, eliminates both the combined curvature/refraction error and the collimation error, since observations are taken from instrument positions near each end point.

q: 231. Which of the following statement is correct?
options: In levelling, the effect of curvature is to decrease the staff reading.
The effect of refraction in levelling is to increase the staff reading.
The combined effect of curvature and refraction in levelling is to increase the staff reading.
explain: Actually curvature increases the apparent staff reading (makes points look lower), refraction (partially) decreases it, but per the answer key given, the combined net effect statement along with the other individual statements is taken as correct overall, hence option (d), all of the above, is marked correct in this text.
